questions.q: What are the three parts every Suricata rule in this lab is built from?
options: An action, a header (protocol, source, direction, destination), and a set of options in parentheses
A source IP, a destination IP, and nothing else
A single content match and nothing more
A vendor name, a signature ID, and a timestamp
questions.explain: Every Suricata rule follows action, header, options — the same structure Lesson 7 introduced, applied here to two real attack patterns.

questions.q: Why does Rule 1 use http.user_agent as a sticky buffer before matching on "sqlmap"?
options: It restricts the content match to just the User-Agent header instead of scanning the entire packet, which is where sqlmap's default signature actually appears
It encrypts the User-Agent header so attackers can't read it
It has no real function and could be removed without changing the rule's behavior
It forces the rule to only match traffic on port 443
questions.explain: Sticky buffers like http.user_agent scope the following content match to one specific protocol field, which is both more accurate and more efficient than scanning the whole packet.

questions.q: In Rule 2, what do the dsize and threshold keywords each contribute to detecting a beacon?
options: dsize flags the small, fixed request size typical of a check-in, while threshold waits for that pattern to repeat a set number of times in a time window before alerting
dsize checks the destination IP, while threshold checks the source port
Both keywords do the same thing and either one alone would work identically
dsize blocks the traffic immediately, while threshold only logs it for later review
questions.explain: dsize catches the small, consistent request size, and threshold is what distinguishes a single odd request from genuine recurring beaconing.

questions.q: Before Rule 2 goes into production, what tuning step does Castellan's SOC take and why?
options: They add an exception for the authorized vulnerability scanner's source IP, because it legitimately hits the same URI pattern during scheduled scans
They remove the threshold keyword because it's unnecessary
They lower the dsize value to catch even more traffic
They disable the rule entirely because beacon detection isn't possible with Suricata
questions.explain: Without that exception, the authorized scanner's own legitimate traffic would trigger false positives on the beacon-detection rule.

questions.q: Why is Rule 2's size-and-frequency approach described as more durable than Rule 1's exact string match?
options: It doesn't depend on a specific tool's default User-Agent string, so it still catches beaconing behavior even if the attacker switches to a different C2 tool
It runs faster than Rule 1 on the same hardware
It requires no sid or rev fields, unlike Rule 1
It only works on encrypted traffic, which Rule 1 cannot inspect at all
questions.explain: Matching on behavioral shape (size and timing) survives changes to the specific tool an attacker uses, unlike a match tied to one tool's default signature.
